summary.text:
East Sussex Fire Authority's Treasury Management Strategy for 2026/27 (33 pages) is a self-contained substantive TMS taken by the Authority on 12 February 2026, from Duncan Savage, Assistant Director Resources / Treasurer — the S112 responsible officer, which is the fire-authority equivalent of s151 (Appendix 1 §2.1, p16). All seven appendices are bundled in the PDF: Scheme of Delegation, Prudential and Treasury Indicators, MRP Policy, MUFG's December 2025 economic overview, Counterparty list, Investment Benchmarking and Glossary. Every figure needed for the loan-book reconciliation and the balance-sheet identity sits in this one document — no companion Q3 or half-year paper is needed.

The loan book reconciles cleanly. Our file, searched under the exact bc-loans name ‘EAST SUSSEX FIRE AUTHORITY’ (a naming trap: ‘East Sussex Fire and Rescue’ returns no match), holds 18 individual PWLB advances totalling £8,495,000 at a coupon-weighted 4.4549%, all MATURITY-profile. Table 2 (p4) prints external borrowing forecast at £8,495k at 31 March 2026 at a weighted 4.46%. Principal ties to the pound; rate ties to two decimal places (4.4549% rounds to 4.45%; the paper prints 4.46% — one basis point of rounding). Table 12 (p21) states ‘All Fire Authority borrowing is at a Fixed Rate’ and §4.8 (p8) confirms ‘No borrowing is subject to early repayment options (LOBO Loan)’ — both consistent with our file. Table 5's (p8) short-maturity schedule (£550k 2026/27, £600k 2027/28, £550k 2028/29) foots against our under-12-months (two loans, £550k combined) and one-to-two-year buckets (one loan, £600k) exactly.

The balance-sheet identity ties to the pound at every forecast year-end. The Authority holds no PFI schemes and no finance leases on the balance sheet today (App. 2 §1.6, p18), so Other Long-Term Liabilities are zero. At 31 March 2026, CFR £10,392k minus external borrowing £8,495k minus OLTL £0 equals £1,897k, and the paper prints 1,897 in Table 3's Under/(Over) borrowing line. The same identity ties for 2026/27 (£3,000k), 2027/28 (£3,000k) and 2028/29 (£2,769k). Four out of four ties are exact.

The Authority sits simultaneously under-borrowed at the balance-sheet identity level (external debt about £3m below CFR across the strategy horizon per Table 3) and as a small net treasury investor (investments £12.600m against external borrowing £8.495m gives £4.105m net cash at 31 March 2026 forecast per Table 2). §4.2.2 (p7) is explicit that this ‘is expected to change from 2026/27 as reserves reduce and borrowing is required in the capital programme’. The capital programme itself steps up from £3.3m (2025/26) to £7.1m (2026/27) and £6.5m (2027/28), with a total three-year borrowing need of £11.0m against a Loans CFR forecast to peak at £18.0m in 2028/29 (§4.2.2, p7). Financing costs as a share of net revenue rise from 2.17% (2025/26) to 2.94% (2028/29) — modest by council standards but on an upward trajectory.

Two testable observations. First, on the DMO's premature repayment curve dated 14 August 2026, our canonical engine prices the book at a net indicative discount of £657,844 (7.7% of principal), with 7 of 18 loans below par and 11 above. The largest discounts sit on four long-dated loans — two £1m loans at 4.45% maturing 2052 and 2053, and two £500k loans at 3.70% maturing 2051 and 2052. Paper §4.7 (p8) says rescheduling is unlikely to be an option during 2026/27 because premature-redemption rate exceeds new-borrowing rate, and that is correct on the repay-and-reborrow frame — our engine gives the same answer on that test. The different frame is repay-without-reborrow, which §4.10 (p8) explicitly opens: ‘Consideration will also be given to identifying if there is any residual potential for making savings by running down investment balances to repay debt prematurely as short term rates on investments are likely to be lower than rates paid on current debt.’ On today's curve, the book as a whole carries a modest discount if repaid without refinance. Recorded as observation with full caveats; never as advice. Only the DMO can quote a binding premature-repayment figure and no MRP or accounting treatment is modelled.

Second, on the rate view tested. MUFG's December 2025 central forecast for Bank Rate at March 2026 was 3.75%, which is exactly where Bank Rate sits today. On the long end, MUFG's March 2026 forecasts of 5.20% (25y PWLB certainty) and 5.80% (50y) are around a full percentage point below where those rates sit at 14 August 2026 (25y 6.46%, 50y 6.27% per DMO notice 314/26 PM). The Bank Rate call landed; the long end has not fallen. That is context on where the paper's central borrowing assumptions have travelled, not a critique.

FRA precedent, from Avon (mg473), Bedfordshire (mg288) and Cheshire (mg292), has generally been to draft cautiously and flag the send question separately. Devon and Somerset FRA (mg280) drafted an email because the reconciliation was to the pound and the discount observation was substantive; East Sussex fits that pattern — loan-book tie is exact, the book carries a discount finding, and the balance-sheet identity ties four out of four year-ends. Duncan Savage's email address is not published anywhere in the paper (Richard Carcas at richard.carcas@eastsussex.gov.uk is the Contact Officer on the front sheet, but at the county council domain, almost certainly the democratic-services contact rather than the finance officer). A draft has been prepared per the session's instruction; the address needs to be found before send.

officer.body:
Duncan,

Apologies for the cold email — PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're a small platform that carries PWLB rates at both daily fixings, monthly local-authority-to-local-authority lending activity, every borrower's PWLB loan book priced daily against the DMO's premature repayment curve, and a lightweight academy for treasury officers and members. All of the data side is free and stays free. There's more in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL] if it helps to circulate.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that read committee papers across every authority in the country, so we can see how an authority's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. Below are a few thoughts on your 12 February strategy paper, offered ahead of the mid-year review to Scrutiny & Audit later in the year. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The strategy is a full one for a document of its size, with all seven appendices bundled, and this is offered in that spirit rather than as a critique.

The reconciliation earns the rest. Our own file, pulled from the DMO borrower schedule under "EAST SUSSEX FIRE AUTHORITY" (not "East Sussex Fire and Rescue", which is a naming quirk we ran into), holds eighteen individual PWLB advances totalling £8,495,000 at a coupon-weighted 4.4549%, all maturity-profile. Your Table 2 prints external borrowing forecast at £8,495k at 31 March 2026 at a weighted 4.46%. Principal ties to the pound with your forecast, and the rate ties to a basis point of rounding. Paragraph 4.8 confirms no LOBO exposure and Table 12 states "All Fire Authority borrowing is at a Fixed Rate" — both of which match what we hold exactly. It's a clean reconciliation and it means anything else we say below is grounded in the same eighteen loans you are working from.

The balance-sheet identity ties as well. With no PFI schemes and no finance leases on the balance sheet today (Appendix 2 paragraph 1.6), Other Long-Term Liabilities are zero, so CFR less external borrowing gives internal borrowing directly. Your Table 3 prints 1,897 at 31 March 2026, then 3,000, 3,000 and 2,769 across the following three year-ends. £10,392 less £8,495 is 1,897; £14,298 less £11,298 is 3,000; £19,437 less £16,437 is 3,000; £18,656 less £15,887 is 2,769. Four out of four year-ends tie to the pound. The under-borrowed position sits at the exactly £3m the strategy narrates.

Two observations, both grounded in figures you have already published.

On paragraph 4.7 and the repayment picture. The paragraph correctly says that on the repay-and-reborrow calculation there is no financial benefit — the PWLB premature repayment rate today sits above the equivalent new-borrowing rate for like tenors, and we get the same answer. What we can price separately is the different frame that paragraph 4.10 itself opens — "identifying if there is any residual potential for making savings by running down investment balances to repay debt prematurely as short term rates on investments are likely to be lower than rates paid on current debt". On today's DMO premature repayment curve (notice 314/26 PM, 14 August 2026) our engine prices the book at a net indicative discount of £657,844 across the eighteen loans, or 7.7% of principal — seven of the eighteen loans below par, eleven above. The single largest discounts are on four long-dated loans: two £1m loans at 4.45% maturing 2052 and 2053, and two £500k loans at 3.70% maturing 2051 and 2052. This is indicative only — the DMO's quote is the only binding one, we model no MRP effect and no accounting treatment, and whether any of it is worth pursuing turns on replacement cost of the cash and the timing of the capital programme, both of which sit outside our model. Recorded as an observation against the paper's own paragraph 4.10, not as a recommendation. Your loan book is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis if it is useful to have alongside.

On the MUFG rate view. MUFG's December 2025 central forecast for Bank Rate at March 2026 (3.75%) has landed exactly — Bank Rate is 3.75% today. On the long end, MUFG's March 2026 forecast rates in Table 1 of 5.20% for 25-year and 5.80% for 50-year sit around a full percentage point below where those rates actually are at 14 August 2026 — 25-year certainty is 6.46% and 50-year is 6.27% on DMO notice 314/26 PM. Bank Rate call landed, long end has not fallen. That is context on where the paper's central borrowing assumptions have travelled in the six months since it was written, not a critique of MUFG or of the strategy. The daily curve and the derived liability benchmark page are at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity, and CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates put the liability benchmark in front of everyone this cycle, so having a version that moves with the market rather than being recalculated annually is worth a look.

A disclosure on our own coverage. We hold PWLB only — the fire authority's book is 100% PWLB per paragraph 4.8 and Table 2, so in this case we hold the whole external debt position, and the reconciliation above is on the complete book. Investment positions, counterparty tables and cash management sit outside what we do.

On training, three courses would fit here — the Liability Benchmark course pitched at fire-authority scale, a session on premature repayment and rescheduling arithmetic that covers the not-reborrow frame in the observation above, and a Prudential and Treasury Code refresher for the mid-year cycle. Everything is free to local authorities and fire authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

If any of this is useful, word of mouth is how we reach colleagues at other authorities — a mention to a peer treasurer in the region does more than any campaign we could run.
